value.text: With less than a week until Election Day, the race for Palm Beach County Commission District 6 is putting some of western Palm Beach County's biggest issues directly before voters. Republican incumbent Sara Baxter and Democratic challenger Katherine Waldron spoke separately with WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman about affordability, development and traffic, transparency and the debate over AI data centers.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Baxter, Waldron make their case to voters The two candidates emerged from their respective primaries and will face each other in the general election. Baxter is seeking another term representing District 6, while Waldron is looking to bring her previous experience at the Port of Palm Beach and in the Florida House to the County Commission.Hoffman has been following the District 6 contest for months. As the race enters its final stretch, he pressed both candidates on how their experience would shape their approach to some of the district's most contentious issues.Baxter is the Republican incumbent. Her time representing District 6 is her first elected political office. She has also been endorsed by President Donald Trump."We're putting in a lot of hard work," Baxter told WPTV reporter Michael Hoffman.Waldron, a Democrat, previously served as a Port of Palm Beach commissioner before serving one term as a state representative."We're out there every day," Waldron told Hoffman.That difference in experience has become part of the choice before voters. Baxter points to her record on the County Commission, while Waldron points to her experience in multiple elected offices.Hoffman asked both candidates about affordability, traffic and development, issues affecting residents across District 6.Waldron argued that transparency has been lacking and said she has heard from residents who don't believe their concerns are being heard."My general sense when I've been out there talking to voters in my district and beyond is that they feel like they're not being heard. They feel like there's not transparency," Waldron told Hoffman.She also questioned whether enough is being done to mitigate the effects of development on surrounding communities."They're not really looking into or trying to mitigate the impact that it will have on the constituents, on schools, on traffic, on quality of life," Waldron said.Baxter pointed voters to her record on the commission, telling Hoffman she has tried to fight for residents while navigating competing opinions within the district."I have always tried to do what's best for the residents and fight for them. And sometimes I have residents on different sides of issues," Baxter said.Baxter said residents can look at her previous votes and commission meetings when deciding whether she has effectively represented them."I think, in my seat particularly, I have a record. People can see what I have fought for. They can watch past commission meetings and know that you'll not find a better fighter for, you know, our district," Baxter said.Baxter also noted that decisions before the County Commission involve seven commissioners, each bringing their own opinions to the table.On one of the most controversial development issues in western Palm Beach County, Baxter and Waldron find themselves on the same side.Both candidates have opposed Project Tango, the proposal for a massive AI data center near the Arden community and a new elementary school.The issue has become part of a broader conversation over data center development in Palm Beach County and what that development could mean for surrounding communities.For Waldron, the Project Tango debate also connects to her broader argument about transparency and how development decisions affect residents.For Baxter, the issue is part of the record she is asking voters to consider as she seeks another term representing District 6.After discussing their differences, Hoffman closed each interview with a different question: What is one thing each candidate respects about her opponent?"I respect anybody who wants to serve the public and represent the public," Waldron told Hoffman.Waldron said she believes elected officials can sometimes face criticism without people appreciating the challenges that come with serving in public office."A lot of times people bash politicians or leaders and stuff like that. And a lot of times, I don't think it's really fair," Waldron said."You can have tough days, and I imagine she's probably had some," Waldron added.Baxter expressed a similar view about the difficulty of representing residents with different opinions."It's definitely not as easy as people might think," Baxter told Hoffman. "You have people with different opinions, as we should. So you're always going to have somebody who's upset because they don't like that, and your people are going to be happy because they like what you stand for.""At the end of the day, we do our best to represent the residents," Baxter said.Despite their differences over how District 6 should be represented, Baxter and Waldron agree on one thing as the race nears its end: They want residents to get out and vote.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Strong surf pounding Palm Beach County’s coastline has damaged the historic Jupiter Civic Center at Carlin Park, forcing the building to close as crews take emergency measures to protect the nearly 100-year-old structure.The impact is hard to miss.The front of the Civic Center is blocked off by caution tape.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Strong surf damages historic Jupiter Civic CenterBehind the building, much of the beach has been washed away, leaving broken branches, eroded sand and steps exposed or damaged along the shoreline.For longtime beachgoers, seeing the damage to a place tied to generations of memories is difficult.When asked how much the Civic Center means to her, Jacqueline Trochinsky said, "Oh, a lot. I have a lot of memories there. Many of my friends have been married there, baby showers."Strong tides and gale-force winds have taken a toll on the historic building.Video shared with WPTV by a beachgoer named Kevin Courtney shows sand eroded from underneath the deck and some of the concrete from the Civic Center collapsed.County crews have now mobilized an emergency contractor, bringing in piles of sand that are being placed along the beach to reinforce the shoreline and try to protect the structure.One Jupiter resident, Bill, said he understands the need for the work."We're fighting a never-ending battle of renourishment here, but I don’t mind seeing my tax dollars go to that," Bill said.For him, the Civic Center has been part of the Jupiter community for decades."It's just been a local scene, hang out for kids when I was in high school in ’73," Bill said.It's uncertain the extent of the damage or when the Civic Center could reopen.When asked what message Trochinsky had for county leaders, she said, "Just take care of us, take care of the locals, including our beach."This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. Lucie River.The developer said the parcel was donated from the northern section of the Newfield development to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect, and preserve South Florida's water resources.WATCH REPORT BELOW: James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality. Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river.WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project."The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project," Fitzgerald said. "Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects."Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.

What looks like an ordinary blue backpack is giving first responders in North Palm Beach a new way to connect with people with autism during an emergency.North Palm Beach Fire Rescue has equipped its fire trucks with Ben's Blue Bags, backpacks filled with sensory and communication tools designed to help first responders interact with people experiencing sensory overstimulation.WATCH REPORT BELOW: North Palm Beach firefighters add sensory bags for autism callsThe bags can include items such as fidget toys, noise-canceling headphones, dry-erase boards, and communication tools that can help someone express what they need or how they are feeling."Fidget toys, fidget spinners, Rubik's Cubes," firefighter Noah Denker said while showing WPTV reporter Christy Waite what is inside one of the bags. "The special thing about these bags is they have communication devices. There's a blank white board they can write on, there's a keyboard so they can type it out, and a how are you feeling chart."For Denker, bringing the bags to North Palm Beach started with a connection close to home. His wife is a fifth-grade teacher who works with children with autism. Seeing how she uses sensory tools with her students inspired Denker to find a way to give first responders similar resources in the field."My wife is a fifth-grade teacher for kids with autism, and she gave me the idea," Denker said. "She has things in her classroom to help with overstimulation before they hit that meltdown stage."That idea led Denker to research Ben's Blue Bags.Ben's Blue Bags is a nonprofit that was founded in 2019 by Matt Kodicek, a captain and paramedic with the Crown Point Fire Department in Indiana and the father of a child on the autism spectrum. The idea was inspired by his son, Ben, after Kodicek saw a need for first responders to have additional tools and training to help people experiencing sensory overstimulation.The organization has distributed more than 700 bags, and they are being used by more than 3,000 first responders across seven states and Canada.Now, some of those bags are riding along on North Palm Beach fire trucks, giving crews immediate access to sensory and communication tools when they respond to a call. The department says North Palm Beach Fire Rescue is the first department in Florida to use Ben's Blue Bags. "We are seeing more and more kids with autism or at least on the spectrum, so we think they will have a big impact when it comes time for us to use them," North Palm Beach Fire Rescue Deputy Chief Anthony Giarrusso said.The department is also hoping the effort eventually extends beyond fire rescue.Denker said they are working with the North Palm Beach Police Department to get the bags into the hands of police officers, giving both agencies access to the tools when they encounter someone who may need them.

On the north end of Corpus Christi, Texas, Craig Street is a new dividing line. Diane Gudmanson and Carol Lowe live on one side. Matilda Rodriguez lives on the other. In January, they will have different representatives in Congress because Republicans redrew Congressional maps. “We can’t even go and talk to our neighbors across the street and say, 'Let’s work together and talk to our representative together,' because we have different representatives in Congress,” Lowe said.“I hate that map,” said Gudmanson.In redrawing District 34, the strategy used “cracking,” a method that divides communities among districts to dilute their electoral influence.In addition to carving out a section of Corpus Christi, which predominantly votes Democrat, the Republican-led Texas Legislature also split parts of the Rio Grande Valley into separate districts, leaving some farmers and ranchers with land and business interests in both.“You're going to have people going in there pulling that damn lever, and they don't have any idea who's who they're voting for, or who's actually going to be representing them,” said rancher Mike England, who is from Mercedes, a town on the district line.Brian Jones, a farmer who lives nearby, said even though the new district is anchored by urban centers Corpus Christi to the north and Brownsville in the south, there’s still a lot of ranching and farming that happens in between. He says whoever wins in the midterms will have to represent agricultural interests as well.The redrawing was done on the political assumption that Latino voters, who voted for Donald Trump in record numbers in Texas in 2024, would vote Republican in 2026.“It’ll backfire,” said Rodriguez.

The Democratic campaign for Alaska's U.S. Senate seat was involved in efforts to place on the ballot a candidate with the same name as Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in a bid to confuse voters in a race that could determine which party controls the chamber, The New York Times reported Wednesday.The newspaper obtained text messages between members of Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign discussing recruiting other people with the same name as the two-term Republican their candidate was running against. They eventually landed on a retired schoolteacher in the small fishing community of Petersburg named Dan J. He made it through the state's August open primary and is one of four candidates on the ranked vote ballot for next Tuesday's general election.Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest and has said he had no contact with Peltola's campaign: “Zero, none, zilch,” he said in June after announcing his run.He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment Wednesday from The Associated Press.A top state elections official ruled Dan J. Sullivan ineligible for the ballot after he declared his candidacy, claiming it was “filed with a purpose to confuse or mislead and to thereby compromise the ballot’s fairness or neutrality.”The case went to the Alaska Supreme Court, which ruled he was qualified to run. Constitution sets out only age, citizenship and residency requirements to run for the Senate.President Donald Trump, who directed his Department of Justice to file a lawsuit last week pre-emptively contesting a Peltola win due to the presence of the second Dan Sullivan, called for legal penalties against Democrats over the situation: “Mary Peltola should suffer the Legal and Political consequences for what she has done,” Trump wrote on his social media site on Wednesday.He added that he didn't think Peltola should be able to run, calling her campaign's alleged act, "ELECTION FRAUD.""The Democrats cheated! They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didn’t know anything about it. That’s perjury," Trump stated. "She shouldn’t be allowed to run, and neither should the FAKE Dan Sullivan."“Alaskans deserve the truth,” said Nate Adams, a spokesperson for Sen. “Mary Peltola, her campaign and her senior advisers colluded with the DSCC, national Democrat lawyers and Alaska Democrat operatives to recruit candidates to deliberately confuse and deceive voters.”Peltola's campaign, in a statement Wednesday, said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” They issued a similar statement in June after Sen. Sullivan questioned the other Sullivan's candidacy.Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick.“The DSCC is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan," the organization said in a statement Wednesday. The Times report said DSCC staffers were on texts with the Peltola campaign discussing the second Sullivan.Legal experts said the report about Democrats appearing to recruit Dan J. Sullivan as a way to potentially confuse voters will have no impact on a lawsuit filed recently by the U.S. President Donald Trump directed the department to file the lawsuit, which seeks to halt certification of a possible Peltola win, citing the presence of the second Dan Sullivan on the ballot.“It’s a dirty campaign trick, and it’s good reason the Alaska Supreme Court should have permitted the candidate to have been removed from the ballot,” said Derek Muller, a Notre Dame law professor. “But now it’s in the hands of the voters, not litigation.”It's not the first time a candidate's appearance on the Alaska ballot has been questioned. In 2024, the state Democratic Party sued to keep off the U.S. House ballot a man with no apparent ties to the state who is serving time in a federal prison in New York. A divided state Supreme Court allowed him to remain on the ballot. The man is running again this year, also in the House race, and is on the Nov. 3 ranked vote general election ballot.The Times story about the recruitment of Dan J. Sullivan is based partly on interviews with Peltola's former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August amid a campaign shake-up. The newspaper said she tried to retract her comments last week. Efforts by the AP to reach Rios were not immediately successful.As of Monday, 46,204 ballots had already been cast in Alaska, according to AP data. Sullivan is listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent. The other Sullivan is listed as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation.

On Election Day, around 100,000 precincts will be up and running, filled with election officials, volunteer poll workers, and potentially some election monitors or observers.Election monitoring has long been part of the US electoral system. Avery Davis-Roberts, the director of the Democracy Program at the Carter Center said, "It's a great way for people to get engaged in the process, right? To understand how elections work, to really sort of learn the nuts and bolts of what goes into running an election.”For 2026, there are a few different types of observers voters could see at their polling site. People there to observe or monitor the election will largely fall a handful camps – partisan poll watchers, nonpartisan observers, volunteers, DOJ election monitors and congressional observers.RELATED STORY | Federal agents are ending up at polling places for reasons unrelated to the electionIn every state except West Virginia, political parties or candidates are allowed to send poll watchers to voting sites.“This does mean ensuring the integrity of elections... but it also means ensuring that their own supporters can vote and from time to time, challenge challenging the eligibility of potential opposition supporters,” explained Mollie Cohen, an associate professor of political science at Purdue University.What exactly partisan poll watchers can do depends on the state. But in 32 states, they can challenge the eligibility of a voter. As Cohen explains, the requirements for those challenges vary by state: "For example, in North Carolina, poll watchers who challenge the eligible eligibility of a voter have to submit an oath under threat of perjury and perjury to an election official in the state of North Carolina is a felony offense. In a place like Nevada, Election Day challenges of voters have are only considered valid if they're based on direct personal knowledge.”Advocacy groups and nonprofits, like the Carter Center, also organize and train poll watchers. Depending on state rules, they could be inside or outside the polling place, but they're there purely to observe and help improve transparency.“All of the observers that you might see have to abide by state law. They shouldn't be interfering in the process. There shouldn't be anything that makes voters feel unsafe or intimidated,” said Davis-Roberts.Also, the Department of Justice is deploying about 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states. It’s a notable increase from the last midterm election, where the department deployed only 388 election monitors in 2022. In a statement to Scripps News, the DOJ said: “Every monitor will merely observe and report any potential violations of federal law to the Department, which will be reviewed after Election Day.”MORE ELECTION NEWS | Why Social Security could become a major issue for the senators elected in 2026Two other types of people voters might see. Volunteers might be outside the ‘electioneering line’ providing sample ballots, information on issues or assisting voters stuck in a long line. You also could see congressional election observers. They are allowed to see every part of the voting process and their observations could even come into play if a race is contested.And election observation will extend beyond November 3. In many states, observers can watch the ballot counting and the procedures for processing mail-in ballot, which is officially called canvassing.

For years, Palm Beach County has faced a shortage of mental health resources for children, leaving families vulnerable. Now, members of the community are stepping up to fill the need.Florida Atlantic University is launching a new program to provide that support for free.WATCH REPORT BELOW: FAU launches free mental health program for childrenThe program, called "OWLS-FLY" (short for Opportunity, Wellness, Leadership & Strength with Families Leading Youth), is being spearheaded by researchers Kelly Emelianchik-Key and Alex Fields inside the education building at FAU. It was made possible by a $1.2 million grant from the Children's Services Council of Palm Beach County.The program will provide free mental health counseling for kids ages 6 through 17 and their families."We provide group counseling, individual counseling, family counseling, and we'll have some different parental supports that are going to take place," Emelianchik-Key said.The space is still coming together with different rooms for family and individual therapy. There's also a room set up to provide care via telehealth. Emelianchik-Key said she anticipates the first clients to be served in January.Fields said the stakes for young people are high."If you don't have solid mental health support, you can't build the foundation for a really healthy and high quality of life down the road," Fields said.The program serves two needs: it helps families who need services, and it provides work experience for the people who are learning to provide them."We've worked with clinicians in the community, specifically for youth with intellectual and developmental disabilities, and I've heard how long their wait lists are, and that they're not able to provide services for months and on out," Fields said.Master's students and graduates will get work experience through the program. Michelle Abarca of the Children's Services Council hopes to take what's learned through FAU's program and scale it in the future."Working with FAU is particularly exciting for us because we are a data-driven organization, and with the research that's going to be taking place at FAU, we hope to learn. We hope to be able to replicate some of this at one point," Abarca said.The program is funded for three years, but Emelianchik-Key and Fields hope to continue it for years to come."To be able to do this is a really great honor," Emelianchik-Key said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Senate to the governor’s mansion, dozens of Black women are on the ballot across the country.Dr. Ndidiamaka Okpareke, a pharmacist and Republican newcomer seeking a New Mexico congressional seat, is one of them.“We need adequate representation at the table so that we can pull our communities forward,” Okpareke told Scripps News.The daughter of Nigerian immigrants and a mother of three, Okpareke would be the first Black woman to represent New Mexico in Congress if she wins her long-shot bid against a three-term incumbent.RELATED STORY | Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challengesSome 1,500 miles away, 25-year-old Courtney McClain is making a similar bid. The Gen Z Democrat is running in South Carolina’s 4th Congressional District in the Upstate, one of the state’s most conservative districts. She is seeking to become the first Black woman the state has sent to Congress.McClain told Scripps News that many people doubted her candidacy at the start.“Now that we are so close to the finish line and with the support that we’ve been able to get people now realize that we can win this race,” McClain said.“STILL CONTINUING TO RUN”Okpareke and McClain are part of a larger group challenging assumptions about Black women’s electability. There are 72 Black women on the midterm ballot, according to data from Rutgers University’s Center for American Women and Politics and Higher Heights. Near majority are Democrats.Four Black women are running for the Senate while 40 Black women nominees are in the running for the lower chamber, two are in the running for governor and 26 are running for other statewide offices.University of Florida professor Sharon Austin told Scripps News these were once officer that women didn't tend to run for, especially women of color.“Now it seems the sky's the limit and more women of color are seeking all offices at all levels,” Austin said.Austin, who has studied Black women in politics, said Black women candidates know the climb to the ballot, let alone victory, is steep.“These are women who know that when they decide to run for office it isn’t going to be easy. They’re going to have to deal with a lot of biases and a lot of bigotry. But many of them are able to overcome it, and they’re still continuing to run,” she said.“There definitely has been progress. There always is going to be bigotry, unfortunately, and there’s always going to be barriers,” Austin added. “But I think there are people in today’s society who are a lot more willing to look beyond race and gender when they cast their votes.”“TAKE YOURSELF OUT OF THE BOX”McClain said she doesn’t want her campaign defined by history-making alone.“Representation isn’t just about what the person looks like, but it’s about what that person can actually bring and do for the community,” McClain added.For Okpareke, a medical professional who says she’s bringing firsthand experience to policy that impacts different communities, representation goes beyond race or gender.“There are boxes that are built for us on both sides of the aisle,” Okpareke said. “We've seen that so often where you align yourself with a certain ideology or a certain way to think and you get boxed in and you can never come out of that.”“So take yourself out of the box, be true to who you are, and stand for the people,” she added.INTERACTIVE | How the midterms could shape the future of Social SecurityKelly Dittmar, director of research at CWAP, told Scripps News the election story this year goes beyond the firsts. Some Black women are leaving Congress, so the overall number may not rise sharply, she said. But the new candidates include younger women and those from different backgrounds who clear new paths and bring complex perspectives to office."We found in our own research that what that means is they're often bringing not only their own voices but also voices from their communities,” Dittmar said. “They’re diversifying the representation among the Black women who are serving.”She said voters are also looking for something new, and women can use the fact that they haven’t been part of the status quo to their advantage.“I think this year we will see a number of cases of success to further prove the case that women can and do win some of the toughest races, that Black women can and do win in majority-white electorates, which has been a bias in a lot of the discussions around when and where Black women should run,” Dittmar said.McClain said that’s the message she is carrying into Election Day.“That excitement. That want for change,” she said. "Not just on being the first Black woman but running on being a candidate that is truly going to represent the Upstate and is truly going to bring change.”“I hope to see a version of America that works for all people, and a version of America that is truly going to be representative of the least of us,” McClain said.Win or lose Tuesday, Okpareke said she hopes to change the conversation about where and when Black women can run for office.“I would just want to inspire anyone from different backgrounds to let them know you can do it,” she said. “You too can stand for and guard and protect and nurture the American dream because it's not going to end with you.”

Early voting ends Saturday, Oct. Lucie, Indian River and Okeechobee counties. Palm Beach County voters have one more day to vote early, with sites open through Sunday, Nov. See also: Sand crews mobilize as king tides, gale-force winds erode Jupiter Civic Center beach On Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, polls will be open from 7 a.m. Voters must cast their ballots at their assigned polling place. Check your location and sample ballot with your county Supervisor of Elections before heading out. Early voting hours Hours vary by county: Palm Beach County: Through Nov. Martin County: Through Oct. Lucie County: Through Oct. Indian River County: Through Oct. to 4 p.m., with extended hours Thursdays. Okeechobee County: Through Oct. During early voting, voters may use any open early voting site in their county. 3, they must go to their assigned polling place. What’s on the ballot Voters across the region will decide races for governor, U.S. The statewide contests include Republican Byron Donalds against Democrat David Jolly for governor, Republican Ashley Moody against Democrat Angie Nixon for U.S. Senate, and Republican James Uthmeier against Democrat Jose Javier Rodriguez for attorney general. Congressional and state legislative races also will appear on ballots. Local races and ballot questions depend on a voter’s address. Palm Beach County voters also should check their congressional district and polling place after recent redistricting. One statewide ballot question is Amendment 3, which would increase the homestead exemption for non-school property taxes and lower the annual cap on assessment increases for certain non-homestead properties. It also would limit how local governments can use property tax revenue. Supporters say it would provide tax relief; local governments and public agencies have warned it could reduce funding for services. A proposed constitutional amendment needs at least 60% voter approval to pass. Vote-by-mail deadline The deadline to request a vote-by-mail ballot was Oct. Returned ballots must reach the local elections office by 7 p.m. on Election Day to be counted. In Palm Beach County, ballots delivered to branch offices must arrive by 5 p.m. Voters can check their sample ballot, polling place and county-specific voting information through their Supervisor of Elections office: Palm Beach County Martin County St. Lucie County Indian River County Okeechobee County

Posted and last updated A funding deadline in 2032 could trigger a 20% cut in benefits unless Congress acts. The senators elected this year will be in office when that moment arrives. Voters focused on gas prices, health care, and foreign policy may be overlooking a slower-moving financial crisis: Social Security. The program that tens of millions of Americans depend on is heading toward a funding shortfall — and the senators winning seats right now will be the ones in Washington when Congress is forced to decide what to do. From debates in Michigan to candidate forums in Maine, the issue is already reshaping how campaigns talk about retirement security. Here s what the deadline means, what s on the table, and what it could mean for your benefits. The math is straightforward — and the consequences are not. Under current law, Social Security s funding is projected to hit a wall in 2032. When that happens, the program would only be able to pay out what it takes in, resulting in an automatic 20% cut to every beneficiary s check unless Congress steps in first. That includes people already retired, people on disability, and survivors who depend on the program. The senators Americans vote into office this year will serve six-year terms — putting them squarely in Washington when that deadline arrives. That means the choices voters make now aren t just about the next budget cycle. They re about who sits at the table when Congress is eventually forced to act. That acknowledgment from a Republican Senate candidate in Michigan reflects just how quickly Social Security has moved from political third rail to campaign centerpiece. From Scripps News Group s debate stage in Detroit to candidate forums in Maine, the program s finances are being debated openly — and candidates are being pressed on what they d actually do. Michigan s Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed has proposed eliminating the income cap on Social Security taxes entirely. Susan Collins has called for a bipartisan commission to study solutions. The distance between those two approaches captures the difficulty Congress will face: the solutions that exist are politically costly, and the window to act is narrowing. The answers may surprise you. That s exactly the kind of knowledge gap the 2032 deadline is closing — fast. The program hasn t faced a moment like this since the 1980s, when Congress waited until the deadline was months away before reaching a deal. History suggests urgency alone doesn t accelerate negotiations in Washington. The political difficulty is real on every proposed fix. Raising the tax cap on incomes above $184,500 would function as a tax increase on higher earners — something many Republicans have resisted. Raising the retirement age above 67 shifts the burden onto workers, particularly those in physically demanding jobs who can t easily work longer. Collins has proposed, delays the hard choices — potentially past the deadline. Verdict: mostly false The program isn t going bankrupt — it would still collect payroll taxes and pay out benefits. But the funding shortfall means it could only cover roughly 80% of promised benefits, resulting in an automatic 20% cut, not a total collapse. Verdict: false Former Social Security Commissioner Martin O Malley was explicit: every current beneficiary could face a 20% reduction in benefits if Congress doesn t act. The cut applies across the board — retirees, disabled recipients, and survivors. Verdict: true O Malley cited polling showing that eliminating or altering the Social Security tax cap is supported by over 80% of people — making it one of the rare proposals with genuine cross-partisan backing. Verdict: false The 1980s presented a similar moment, and Congress ultimately reached a deal — though not until the deadline was just months away. That precedent cuts both ways: a fix is possible, but it may not come early. A report from the Trump administration found that lower fertility rates, higher deportations, and tax changes have contributed to fewer dollars flowing into Social Security. The finding is notable because it ties specific policy decisions — not just demographic trends — to the program s funding pressures. Lower fertility rates mean fewer workers entering the system over time. Higher deportations reduce the number of workers contributing payroll taxes. And tax changes can shift how income is classified, affecting how much revenue flows to the program. Together, these factors compound the structural funding gap that Congress will eventually need to address. Social Security matters to every corner of America because it is one of the few federal programs that touches nearly every household — whether through a grandparent s retirement check, a disabled family member s monthly benefit, or a worker s paycheck deductions that fund it all. The senators elected now won t just inherit an abstract policy debate. They ll inherit a deadline with a specific date and a specific consequence: a 20% cut to benefits that tens of millions of Americans are counting on. The 1980s showed that Congress can act — but also that it tends to wait until the last possible moment. With the 2032 deadline now within a single Senate term, the voters who cast ballots this year are, in a very real sense, choosing who will be in the room when the deal gets made — or doesn t.

President Donald Trump is crisscrossing the campaign trail in the final days before the midterm elections, making stops in Texas, Ohio and South Carolina as Republicans fight to hold key seats.Trump campaigned in Texas on Tuesday, where Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton is locked in a competitive race against Democrat James Talarico. While there, Trump also took time to talk about another prominent Texas Republican, Sen. Ted Cruz.Trump joked that Cruz would be an easy choice to confirm if a seat opened on the U.S. Supreme Court.“I would pick Ted Cruz to be the next Supreme Court justice,” Trump said. “And I wouldn’t have to worry about, I wouldn’t even have to make a phone call.”Trump went on to joke that Cruz would receive unanimous support for an unusual reason.RELATED STORY | Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges“The Democrats will 100% vote for it because they hate the guy and they want to get rid of him,” Trump said. “And the Republicans would 100% vote for it because they can’t stand him. They would like to get rid of him. So I’d get 100% of the vote.”Trump’s Texas appearance was part of a late campaign push aimed at turning out Republican voters ahead of Election Day. He also focused on energy policy, announcing a move to loosen methane rules for oil and gas producers. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana The vote follows an earlier commission meeting in which officials advanced the proposed moratorium for further consideration. Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.

Lucie County sheriff’s deputy turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued in connection with an off-duty crash in Vero Beach, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office. Read also: Road Ranger killed, hit at crash scene on I-95 near Lantana Road Deputy Tyler Horstman was driving an agency vehicle when he was involved in the crash on March 1, the sheriff’s office said. On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. Vero Beach police say Horstman was driving at 63 mph in a posted 35 mph zone and entered the intersection on a green light. The other driver entered the intersection against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital, and the infant was not injured. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor of alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

Floodwaters have inundated parking spaces, roads and walkways at a Boynton Beach condominium complex, leaving residents struggling to get in and out as king tides, strong onshore winds and heavy rain push water onto the property.At Coastal Towers Condominium Apartments, located at 730 E. She requested a review of the conditions and clarification on what corrective measures could help prevent or reduce future flooding.The City of Boynton Beach said it is aware of the flooding at Coastal Towers and has had crews monitoring and documenting affected areas.In a statement to WPTV, the city said it has been responding as needed, including providing support from its police and fire rescue departments and supplying sandbags.City staff have also been in contact with the condominium association and FDOT, which scheduled a site visit to observe conditions during the king tide.The city said communities throughout South Florida face similar challenges when king tides combine with onshore winds and heavy rainfall, pushing water above levels that much of the region's infrastructure was built to handle.Addressing the flooding, the city said, will require coordination among public agencies and private property owners."The City remains committed to working with the association and these partners," the statement said.While the city has outlined its immediate response, it has not announced specific long-term repairs or a timeline for mitigation at Coastal Towers.For residents, the immediate concern remains navigating the floodwaters — and determining what can be done to reduce the risk of similar conditions during future king tides.

"I can no longer work, drive, attend to my obligations, develop my company, and continue building my life. I can no longer go out without the fear of being stopped and detained by ICE agents. They don't want to get involved. They're afraid that they will be deported and detained. A new Boys & Girls Club officially opened its doors Tuesday in West Palm Beach, bringing a new place for hundreds of children and teens to learn, explore their interests and prepare for their futures.The Julie & Mike Connors Boys & Girls Club, located at 1150 Southern Blvd., celebrated its grand opening after years of planning.WATCH REPORT BELOW:"To have this come to fruition is more beautiful than I ever thought it could be," Julie Connors said during the celebration.The $17 million, 31,000-square-foot facility is the 21st location for the Boys & Girls Clubs of Palm Beach County and is expected to serve approximately 800 children and teens each year, with about 220 attending daily. Women's hockey is growing in South Florida, from the pee-wee level all the way up to the college level, and the University of Miami Women's Hockey Club team is part of that surge.Head coach Justina Holland, a former player, rebooted the women's hockey club program at the University of Miami in 2021. I had to find some girls that wanted to play. I did buy jerseys, get ice time, like everything. Then we got it going, and you get teams like Georgia, Alabama, Auburn, and we're slowly building up the South to what it is right now," Holland said.This year, the Canes have 14 players, and Holland credits social media for helping to spread the word and getting more students on skates. Blue Repose Foundation is launching a pilot program designed to help law enforcement officers and other public safety professionals recover from occupational stress through weekly float sessions, peer support and coping techniques.The startup nonprofit introduced the program at Float8 in Delray Beach, where Blue Repose Founder and President Bridget Coghlan discussed the pressures public safety professionals can encounter and the stigma that may prevent some from seeking support.“With our field, of course, we're exposed to traumas, long shift hours, and things of that nature,” Coghlan said. “We don't like to say mental health, so we just want to take care of the person and give them resources to do so within their professional life and their personal life at home.”Coghlan said the pilot will include five participants during its initial monthlong run at Transitions Wellness and Performance Center in Juno Beach.“They'll get a float session, one per week, followed by peer support and other coping decompression techniques to follow and hopefully it'll help them out,” Coghlan said.The program is part of Blue Repose Foundation’s developing mission to provide private, nonclinical restorative opportunities to law enforcement officers, corrections professionals and others working in public safety.Blue Repose says the foundation is being established in Martin County, with an initial focus on serving the Treasure Coast and Palm Beach County. Kristen Neves, the foundation’s director of community engagement and partnerships, said Blue Repose is seeking financial support to launch the pilot.“We're really looking for the community support right now to fund this program and get this pilot program up and going,” Neves said. “We just really want to get this out there and get those law enforcement supported.”Information about contributing to the program is available on the Blue Repose Foundation website.Float8 owner Matt Beck said the Delray Beach studio uses float cabins rather than pods.Float cabins contain shallow water with a high concentration of Epsom salt, allowing a person to remain buoyant. The private environment also reduces outside light, sound and other stimulation.“By reducing the effects of gravity and external stimulation on the body, it helps induce a meditative state, downregulate your nervous system, and help you recover from those stressful situations that our law enforcement officers face so often,” Beck said.Blue Repose describes the float experience as one component of a broader program that will include peer support and additional coping and decompression techniques.Public safety professionals can encounter trauma, long shifts, and sustained stress while serving their communities. Blue Repose’s pilot reflects an effort to give participants structured time to decompress while connecting them with support beyond the float cabin.The initial program will allow Blue Repose to begin evaluating its approach with a small group of participants as the nonprofit works to secure community funding.The foundation’s broader goal is to help professionals take care of themselves in both their working and personal lives while making recovery a more accepted part of public service.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil.The stunning move came after 48 hours in which Bolsonaro refused to concede to Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and then threatened to attempt to annul the election result.Bolsonaro's father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later. said that it would grant visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family. Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, visited the White House in May.Bolsonaro first fled from Brazil to Argentina and then Ecuador alongside his wife and two daughters, Argentina's migration authority said Wednesday — a day after the 45-year-old senator and his family were granted United States visas by the Trump administration.Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil's Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. The court had ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday — two days after he lost the vote to Lula. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport.Argentina's migration authority said Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and his daughters Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro crossed into the country at 10:50 p.m. They entered via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a primary border checkpoint linking Brazil to Argentina's northeastern province of Misiones."Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country," the Argentine migration authority said on X.The authority said that at 11:30 p.m. local time, shortly after clearing immigration control, the four boarded a private charter flight operated by aviation company Baires Fly S.A. According to the filed flight plan, the aircraft departed for Guayaquil, Ecuador.The move is almost certain to cause a big diplomatic rift between Lula and Argentine President Javier Milei, a Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to take part in Bolsonaro's campaign.Bolsonaro lands in MiamiFlight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed that a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro's landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, before taking off minutes later for Miami-Opa locka Executive Airport. The plane carrying Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami at around 9:30 a.m. EST.Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, told several dozen supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia before the plane landed that he didn't have precise information about Bolsonaro's whereabouts, but said he had left Brazil."I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true," Lula said. "This act of leaving Brazil is shameful."Paulo Figueiredo, a close Bolsonaro ally who lives in the U.S., said in a short statement that he can't confirm information from foreign authorities, but added "Flávio Bolsonaro is well, in security and resting with his family." Figueiredo also said there would be a press conference Thursday in Miami to discuss the case.Representatives of Brazil's government didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press.U.S. President Donald Trump said early Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., calling him and his family "fine people.""The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after returning from campaigning in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate, but stressed that he didn't endorse the election results.Leaders all over the world and the Organization of American States, or OAS, endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round.On Tuesday, Milei's administration spokesman Adrián Ravier said "there is no asylum request (from Bolsonaro) and there is nothing more to add."Bolsonaro visited his father, who is under house arrest, before leaving BrazilThe defeated candidate was served with a Supreme Court order to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.After that defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.Flávio Bolsonaro said on Monday in a video that he was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court.Brazil's Supreme Court is investigating Bolsonaro for allegedly using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In a separate case, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker.

Martin County commissioners voted to temporarily halt new applications for large data centers in unincorporated areas of the county for one year on Tuesday. The vote passed 4-0 among Martin County commissioners. The decision gives county officials time to develop regulations governing large data centers, which have raised concerns about electricity consumption and environmental impacts. See also: Corvette, Ferrari take baths as king tides flood West Palm Beach, Lantana The vote follows an earlier commission meeting in which officials advanced the proposed moratorium for further consideration. The temporary pause applies to new applications for large data centers in areas outside city limits, not throughout the entire county. County officials plan to use the one-year period to review and develop rules for future large data center proposals.

WPTV has been following flooding on the Treasure Coast caused by strong winds and king tides on Monday.In Martin County, off Dyer Point Road in Palm City, parts of the area were completely underwater.WATCH BELOW: Flooding swamps parts of Palm City amid king tides, strong windsTerresa Baldwin, who lives off the roadway, said it was flooded for a few hours, but water has since retreated."You could smell the sewage; it was really stinky, it was bad," Baldwin said. "There were dead copperheads, so the snakes are coming out. They're getting flushed out with the water."Baldwin said she was also dealing with flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals.She showed WPTV the water over her dock and in her new patio."The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that," Baldwin said.Despite the water going down, she is still worried about what could happen in the next few days."The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see," Baldwin said. With high tide later Monday night, the sheriff’s office told WPTV the situation could get worse.Lt. Dave Rosko said they have three high-water vehicles ready for rescue efforts and urged neighbors to think twice before driving through the water."Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters," Rosko said. "If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety."Rosko said neighbors living in coastal communities should be aware of future tides before traveling.

Developer Mattamy Homes is transferring 125 acres to Martin County in support of restoring the St. Lucie River.The developer said the parcel was donated from the northern section of the Newfield development to the Comprehensive Everglades Restoration Plan, a federal plan to restore, protect, and preserve South Florida's water resources.WATCH REPORT BELOW: James Fitzgerald, vice president of community development for Mattamy Homes Southeast Florida Division, said the land will have the capacity to host large amounts of muck that will need to be dredged out of the St. Lucie River to improve water quality. Fitzgerald said the Florida Inland Navigation District (FIND) is also donating an adjacent 125 acres. Combined, Fitzgerald said the 250 acres can hold 2.4 million cubic yards of muck from the river.WPTV asked Fitzgerald what happens to the muck after the removal project."The muck will dry out, and we're hoping at some point in the future that land can be used as a recreational project," Fitzgerald said. "Or perhaps, depending on the needs of the county, in some other future environmental restoration projects."Fitzgerald said the project to remove the muck will begin once federal funding is authorized.

By a 4-0 vote, commissioners in Martin County on Tuesday unanimously passed a one-year moratorium on data centers as county leaders consider how to handle future development of the facilities. This was the second reading after commissioners moved forward with the moratorium during a meeting held Oct. Tuesday’s vote comes after Martin County recently received an application to build its first data center proposed in unincorporated Martin County. That application is for the construction of a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95. However, because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it will not be affected by Tuesday’s vote. The proposal comes amid residents’ concerns about the future of data center development.

Martin County commissioners unanimously voted during a second public hearing to implement a one-year moratorium on large-scale data center applications, giving staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. During the hearing, every resident who spoke during public comment opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," said Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades. "I don’t want to spend another year or longer where somebody that I know is trying to do me great bodily harm. Folks, it’s in your hands. These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," said resident Richard Miller. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed there is an applicant for a data center. "One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. The application for the Florida Gateway Project was submitted on Oct. 12, with the first public hearing held the following day. "We got the information late on the Monday before the 13th ... so, I didn't have the information in advance of the 13th. At the meeting on the 13th, I disclosed to everybody that I had just found out about it. I'm sorry, Commissioner, we did alert the commission as soon as we could," said County Attorney Elysse A. "I understand, but somebody took the money on this date is what I'm trying to say. Doesn't anybody talk to anybody here?" Vargas said. The application will go through the development review process, which staff said is expected to take a year. Aside from this application, there are currently no other large-scale data center applications pending. Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he threatened to file lawsuits and ethics complaints against State Rep. Meg Weinberger unless she publicly apologized and backed his push for government audits, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Offic e probable cause affidavit. Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, was booked Oct. He faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. The charges are allegations; Pizzarelli is presumed innocent unless proven guilty. Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9 and offered to leave her out of lawsuits and ethics complaints he said he planned to file if she issued a swift public apology. He also proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat, writing that he did not plan to name her in the complaints but that can change, and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, Pizzarelli transmitted a voice memo May 18th, 2026, directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone in which he stated, among other things: "I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice," "I'm doing the lawsuits," and "you don't know what I can do." The affidavit says Pizzarelli wanted Weinberger to support audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and pursue investigations into government contracting. Weinberger told investigators she had never met him, did not represent him and had no authority over St. She said she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family’s, according to the affidavit. Pizzarelli told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he was seeking an apology over an incident in which she had been copied on an email, and was trying to get her support for his complaints. He had not filed a lawsuit or ethics complaint against her at the time of his interview, the affidavit says. See also: Florida woman convicted in $8.6 million Medicare fraud scheme The affidavit says the investigation found probable cause for the charges after reviewing emails, a May voice message and evidence from electronic devices. Prior accusation of threats In 2025, Pizzarelli was accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies say the communications escalated in tone and content, which raised concern among officials. In the emails he sent, he allegedly using threatening language that included being "ruthless" and making allusions to "murder charges where applicable." Pizzarelli was arrested and booked on counts of intimidation - sending written threats to kill or injure. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from the 2025 case had been dropped. Weinberger, running for reelection, faced intimidation in 2024 Weinberger, a first-term Republican, represents Florida House District 94 in Palm Beach County, according to the Florida House. Weinberger’s campaign faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election. Nicholas Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library. Farley told detectives that seeing Weinberger campaign posters triggered his remarks. The case involved Farley, not Pizzarelli. Absolutely it’s very scary we’re dealing with this. It’s just no way to live and maybe he opens his eyes and realize that we’re just all people doesn’t matter your religion or skin color, Weinberger said at the time. Weinberger is seeking reelection on Tuesday. She faces Democrat Elizabeth Holmes and Doug Barrow (no party affiliation). Related: Early voting ends this weekend across Palm Beach County and the Treasure Coast She was behind the bill that pushed to rename PBIA in honor of President Donald Trump. House District 94 is entirely within Palm Beach County. It stretches from the western Glades communities of Belle Glade, Pahokee and South Bay through areas such as Westlake, Loxahatchee Groves, The Acreage and Jupiter Farms, and includes parts of several eastern communities, including West Palm Beach, Palm Beach Gardens, Jupiter and Royal Palm Beach.
