Family and friends are mourning St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge, a man those closest to him describe as endlessly positive and devoted to serving his community. A funeral procession for Hodge left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Lucie County Sheriff's Office went to the station at 7:25 a.m. 24, regarding a "full cardiac arrest," and Hoge was taken to HCA Florida Lawnwood Hospital. His death comes about 15 months after his younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. After his brother’s death, Austin spent months searching for answers. He told CBS12 News in January that Jarius caught the flu from a patient and died hours after arriving at Cleveland Clinic Tradition Hospital in Port St. Lucie, struggling to breathe. Austin said medical records showed doctors made critical mistakes, including needing three attempts to intubate his brother. CBS12 reached out to the hospital at the time and did not receive a response before that story was published. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, Florida’s so-called free kill law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin pushed state lawmakers to repeal it and started a petition in his brother’s honor. He said the fight was about accountability, not money. Bernard Taylor has known Austin since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior and Austin a freshman when they met at the Boys and Girls Club, where Taylor worked as a counselor and Austin was one of the kids he mentored. Taylor said Austin always wanted to keep up with the older kids, and the two formed a bond that lasted for years. Later, when Taylor decided to change careers, Austin was one of the first people he called. Taylor said Austin supported him through becoming a firefighter, from answering questions to helping him with his conditioning. Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it, Taylor said. Taylor said he spoke with Austin about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he is most heartbroken for Austin’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. That’s one of the strongest people I’ve ever met in my life. I don’t know if I can hold it together if I was her, Taylor said. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Austin’s mother, said she has been by her side and that the family is leaning on its faith and a strong circle of support. I say on my watch, I’m not going to let you die. You’re going to live, and we’re going to get through this, Hill said of what she has told Austin’s mother. Hill said that faith is what is carrying the family now. See also: King tides cause coastal flooding, beach closures in Palm Beach County and Treasure Coast We believe God even in this. We believe God, and we stand on the promises because they won’t fail, Hill said. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin for his love of serving others. He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community, Taylor said. Lucie County Fire District has not released details about Austin Hodge’s death.

Lucie County firefighters and community members gathered to honor firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, escorting him through the community he served after the fire district said he died Saturday and is being honored with a line-of-duty death designation.WATCH: St. Lucie County Honors Firefighter-Paramedic Austin HodgeHodge served the St. Lucie County Fire District for more than nine years. According to the district, he was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse during shift change.Firefighters escorted Hodge from the medical examiner's office to the funeral home as colleagues and community members paid their respects along his final journey through Fort Pierce.Dr. Aleta Paschal, who worked alongside Hodge outside the fire district, described him as someone whose personality made an impression on those around him."Austin is just a bright light," Paschal said. He had the biggest bear hugs. Everybody loved him."Paschal said Hodge had a way of making the people around him feel welcomed."Anybody he interacted with, he made you feel like family for sure," she said.Hodge's work caring for people extended beyond his role as a firefighter-paramedic.Paschal said Hodge also worked as a respiratory therapist, where the two cared for critically ill patients together."Everybody loved him," Paschal said. "He was a critical part of our team. He's going to be very missed at the hospital."Within the St. Lucie County Fire District, Hodge also served on the Honor Guard and the district's Firefighter Challenge Team.Those roles added to a legacy of service that spanned more than nine years with the district.As Hodge's colleagues escorted him through Fort Pierce, Paschal said she hopes people remember the qualities that made him special to those who knew him."Remember his smile. Remember his presence," Paschal said. "Just remember his strength and who he was."The procession offered firefighters, colleagues and members of the community a chance to pay tribute to someone who spent years helping others, both at the fire district and in health care.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Lucie County Fire District firefighter who died unexpectedly Saturday morning has been identified as Austin Hodge, a firefighter paramedic and nine-year veteran of the department.The fire district announced Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital and passed away.WATCH REPORT BELOW: St. Lucie County firefighter dies on duty"Today, our St. Lucie County Fire District family mourns the loss of one of our own," the district said in a statement. In the hours following his death, firefighters, the department's Honor Guard and fellow first responders gathered to honor Hodge and support one another. The district said the response reflected the strong bond shared throughout the fire service. The district thanked the St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Fort Pierce Police Department, Port St. Lucie Police Department and peer support teams from Martin and Indian River counties for providing assistance and standing alongside firefighters during the difficult day."Together, they offered strength, compassion, and support while ensuring Austin was honored with the dignity and respect he deserves," the district said. The district said its thoughts are with Hodge's family, loved ones and everyone who served alongside him. They respectfully ask that Hodge's family be given privacy during this time."We are deeply grateful to our fellow first responders and community for the outpouring of support during this tremendous loss," the district said. "Today and always, we stand together." The tragedy comes more than a year after the community mourned the sudden loss of his brother, Jarius Hodge, 26, who was also a St. Lucie County firefighter and died from septic shock in July 2025.The district said it will share information on funeral and memorial services in coordination with the family when it becomes available.

Lucie County Fire District is honoring the life and service of firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died Saturday while on duty. On Monday afternoon, firefighters escorted Hodge’s body from the medical examiner’s office to a funeral home in Fort Pierce. Tears, respect and a sense of loss were visible on the faces of those gathered to pay tribute. FIREFIGHTER MOURNED: Family honors late St. Lucie County firefighter’s birthday with cookout and balloon release His fellow firefighters, friends and members of the community came together to honor Hodge’s more than nine years of service. Diana Harrison, who has known Hodge’s mother since the early 1990s, shared her memories of him. “So, we actually homeschooled our kids together. Austin was just a little bitty guy back then,” Harrison said. Friends and coworkers expressed the heartbreak of losing Hodge, especially as his brother, Jarius Hodge, also a firefighter-paramedic with the St. Lucie County Fire District, died last year after falling ill while on duty. “I have no words, there’s no words, and the brokenness, the sadness — you can’t imagine losing not one son but two sons,” Harrison said. The fire district reported that Austin Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse during a shift change Saturday. Crews immediately began life-saving measures, but Hodge later died at the hospital. Lucie County Fire District holds procession for firefighter Austin Hodge Deep Dive: WPBF 25 News Investigates Hodge joined the district’s firefighter challenge team in 2018 and helped the team win a world championship in 2021. "He was always a giver, even from a little bitty kid, you know. And if I remember right, even when he was a little kid, he wanted to be a firefighter, and then that's what he became," Harrison said. Howard Dunn Jr., founder of the Howard Dunn Jr. Foundation, which supports first responders, shared his personal connection to Hodge. “A couple of years ago I had a close call, and when the rescue came to me, I met Austin. I had an emergency; they transported me to the hospital. He made me feel better — I forgot what I was going for,” Dunn said. Retired lieutenant and former fire district chaplain Thomas Neiman reflected on the Hodge family’s impact on the community. “Knowing that we saw those kids as grade school kids in the library for our homeschool co-op meetings,” Neiman said. “And of course, we can’t begin to imagine what the family and mom and dad are going through, but we’re holding on to them as best we can, and they know we love them." Funeral arrangements for Austin Hodge have not yet been announced. Stay up-to-date: The latest headlines and weather from WPBF 25

Indian River County’s sea turtles broke a record. The county documented 14,083 nests as of Thursday, its highest total ever recorded. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen credits decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. This is actually a really big deal because what we’re seeing is decades of conservation paying off, Whalen said. But the record season is facing a rough finish. Powerful waves and high tides are eroding beaches, threatening some remaining nests. Loggerheads lead the record season The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. The total surpassed the previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Whalen. Loggerheads drove much of that increase. They’re dominating with 10,000 nests across our entire coastline, which is an insane number, Whalen said. The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County deputy charged with DUI after Vero Beach crash that injured woman, son
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff's detective Tyler Horstman has been charged with DUI following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that seriously injured a woman and hospitalized her son. He surrendered Monday at the Indian River County Jail and was placed on unpaid administrative leave.

Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying the woman and her son at Beachland Boulevard and A1A, investigators said. Investigators determined that the SUV's driver ran a red light and Horstman had a green light. Police said the pickup was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash.

All three people were hospitalized. The child was later released, while the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. Police said the crash could have been fatal.

Investigators determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. According to the affidavit, he said during his assessment that he had consumed “a few beers” earlier in the evening. Police said the investigation took several months as investigators worked through search warrants, subpoenas and records.

Horstman faces several charges, including DUI. St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Horstman's unpaid administrative leave followed agency policy. In a statement, the sheriff said employees are expected to follow the laws they uphold and must be held accountable through the appropriate process when accused of violating that responsibility.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie man arrested, accused of trying to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger
cards.teaser: Investigators say Anthony Pizzarelli demanded an apology and support for government audits, including in St. Lucie County. He denied using his communications as leverage.
cards.body:
A Port St. Lucie man was arrested on charges alleging he tried to extort State Rep. Meg Weinberger by threatening lawsuits and ethics complaints unless she publicly apologized and supported government audits, including in St. Lucie County. The allegations against Anthony Pizzarelli, 50, are outlined in a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office probable cause affidavit.

Pizzarelli faces charges of extortion, using a two-way communication device to facilitate a felony, and harassing an elected official, according to the affidavit. He told investigators he viewed his communications as good faith notices and denied using them to leverage Weinberger. He said he wanted an apology over an incident involving an email on which she had been copied and was seeking her support for his complaints. He is presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

Investigators say Pizzarelli emailed Weinberger on Feb. 9, offering to leave her out of planned lawsuits and ethics complaints if she issued a swift public apology. He proposed wording for the apology. In an April 6 email, he allegedly renewed the threat and urged her to help with his audit campaign. According to the affidavit, he wanted audits of Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties and investigations into government contracting.

The affidavit says Pizzarelli sent a voice memo directly to Weinberger's personal cell phone on May 18, 2026. Among his statements were “I'm an angry person, so I'm not being nice,” and “you don't know what I can do.” Weinberger told investigators she viewed the messages as threats and feared for her safety and her family's safety. A first-term Republican, she represents Florida House District 94, which is entirely within Palm Beach County.

In 2025, Pizzarelli was arrested after being accused of sending threatening emails to St. Lucie County commissioners. Deputies said the communications escalated in tone and content, raising concern among officials. In the current affidavit, Pizzarelli told investigators that all charges from that case had been dropped.

Weinberger's campaign also faced a separate voter intimidation case during the 2024 election involving Nicholas Farley, not Pizzarelli. Farley was arrested after a campaign volunteer said he yelled antisemitic slurs at her and drove threateningly near early voters outside the Acreage Branch Library.

hero.headline: Murray Middle School breaks ground on $33 million rebuilding phase
hero.body:
Murray Middle School has broken ground on a $33 million rebuilding phase that will replace storm-damaged spaces and move displaced students and programs out of portable classrooms, according to Martin County school officials. The project follows damage to three main buildings from a tornado spawned by Hurricane Milton.

School officials said about $33 million has been approved for the second phase of the campus project. The work includes new learning spaces, a performing arts wing and renovations to the gym. The gym is expected to be completed by August 2027, with the new buildings expected to be finished by December 2027. Principal Tiffany Roth said the project includes a media center, an art room and an agriculture room, along with rooms for band and choir in the performing arts wing.

Students and staff gathered for the groundbreaking as rebuilding continued. Martin County Superintendent Michael Maine said improvements to Murray Middle School were planned before Hurricane Milton, but the tornado damage made the work more urgent. “When Hurricane Milton came through and spawned the tornado, it took down three of our main buildings that we rely on every single day,” Maine said. “We couldn't have our students displaced in portables any longer than we needed to.”

Choir was among the programs displaced by the storm. Dr. Anita Caswell, Murray Middle School's choir and drama director, said the storm destroyed decades of program materials, including costumes and drama props. “It was 60 years of drama props,” Caswell said. Her students continued singing in a portable classroom, and she said the choir earned straight superior ratings that year.

For student Nicholas Lowe, the move meant adjusting to a different learning environment. “It was a big change, but also I had to adapt to it to, like, be better for the choir,” Lowe said. Roth said she hopes the completed campus will give students a renewed sense of pride in being Murray Lions.

cards.headline: Siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter found unresponsive in bunk
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s siblings say the firefighter-paramedic appeared normal hours before he was found unresponsive at the firehouse. They are seeking answers about his death.
cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died on duty Oct. 24, say the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk early that morning. They are seeking answers about his final hours, and his family says they do not yet know what caused his death. His sister, Alexis Hodge, said relatives were told he had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. In addition to his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, his family said.

Javan said the family wants to understand the events leading to Austin’s death. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” he said. Alexis said relatives want to know who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Austin’s death comes just over a year after the death of his 26-year-old brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. Relatives raised concerns about the medical care Jairus received, and Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said.

Alexis and Javan said they intend to carry on both brothers’ legacy. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. “The love I have for them is unimaginable. It has no bounds.”

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective accused of speeding in Vero Beach DUI crash
hero.teaser: An arrest report says the woman in the other vehicle suffered a traumatic brain injury. The Sheriff’s Office has put its internal investigation on hold pending the criminal case.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Detective Tyler Horstman is accused of driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone before a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that left another driver with a traumatic brain injury. The allegations are detailed in an arrest report tied to the felony DUI case against Horstman, who turned himself in Monday afternoon after a warrant was issued.

The crash happened about 11:25 p.m. at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. According to the arrest report, Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he struck a Chevy Equinox carrying a woman and an infant. Vero Beach police say Horstman entered the intersection on a green light and the other driver entered against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital. The report describes the woman’s injury as “a traumatic brain injury” and says the infant was alert and responsive.

The arrest report says Horstman acknowledged having a few beers earlier in the evening. It describes a “faint odor of alcohol on his breath” and says he was “lethargic and dazed” and “drowsy and periodically dozing off.” Blood-test results showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit, according to the Sheriff’s Office.

The Sheriff’s Office received those results September 9, and Horstman was placed on administrative leave September 15. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation.

The felony warrant issued Monday lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9.

Read also: Road Ranger killed, hit at crash scene on I-95 near Lantana Road Deputy Tyler Horstman was driving an agency vehicle when he was involved in the crash on March 1, the sheriff’s office said. On September 9, the Sheriff’s Office received Horstman’s blood-test results. They showed a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246, more than three times Florida’s legal limit. According to the arrest report, March 1 at about 11:25pm at the intersection of Beachland Boulevard and A1A in Vero Beach, Horstman was off-duty driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he hit a Chevy Equinox with a woman and an infant inside. Vero Beach police say Horstman was driving at 63 mph in a posted 35 mph zone and entered the intersection on a green light. The other driver entered the intersection against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital, and the infant was not injured. The arrest report says: "Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening." It says Horstman had a "faint odor of alcohol on his breath" and it says Horstman was "lethargic and dazed" and that he was "drowsy and periodically dozing off." The woman in the vehicle he hit suffered "a traumatic brain injury" and the infant was alert and responsive. The arrest report says Horstman had a blood-alcohol level of .246, which is three times the legal limit at which a person is considered too impaired to drive in Florida. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15, according to the St. A felony arrest warrant was issued Monday. It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and later posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his death after the 34-year-old died while on duty Oct. 24. His siblings, Alexis Hodge and Javan Hodge, want to understand what happened in his final hours and what caused his death.

He had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes, according to the account relayed to them. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and Javan gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, his family said.

Both siblings said they are determined to make Austin and Jairus proud. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. “The love I have for them is unimaginable. It has no bounds.”

hero.headline: Kanner Highway data center exempt from Martin County's one-year application pause
hero.body:
The Florida Gateway Project, a proposed data center off Kanner Highway, remains exempt from the one-year pause on large-scale data center applications that Martin County commissioners unanimously approved at a second public hearing. County staff expect the proposal’s development review to take a year, even as the moratorium pauses other applications.

The Florida Gateway Project application was submitted Oct. 12, one day before commissioners held the first public hearing on the moratorium. The county attorney said the information arrived late the day before that hearing and that commissioners were alerted as soon as possible. Commissioner Blake Capps confirmed during the second hearing that the county had received a data center application on Kanner Highway. The proposal will proceed through the county’s development review process.

The moratorium gives staff time to study potential environmental impacts and establish rules for future projects. Every resident who spoke during public comment at the second hearing opposed the possibility of data centers in the county. Casey Darling, policy director for Friends of the Everglades, called for further study. "We simply do not have enough information on what we may be introducing to this ecologically sensitive region and the world's most extensive restoration effort. We need more study and the evaluation of potential impacts, especially in the 16-county greater Everglades region," Darling said.

A resident who said they live one mile from the proposed Florida Gateway Project raised concerns about its scale, electricity demand and potential water use. Resident Richard Miller also objected to locating data centers near people’s homes. "These things are not to be near people that are trying to conduct their ordinary lives," Miller said.

"One of them is the Florida Gateway Project, where this one project has been ... a data center application has come on Kanner Highway," Capps said. A resident who lives near the proposed site raised concerns about the scale of the project. "I happen to live one mile from this new proposed mega center, 100 MW, and 100 MW is like unbelievable to power 100,000 homes, and that's going to be a mile from me. Who knows how much water it's going to use," the resident said. Commissioner Vargas expressed frustration with the application process. "I was not too happy about hearing this application. I even requested the receipt, which I have here in my hand, and the date ... We should give them back and say they don't want you here. It's okay, you go elsewhere," Vargas said. hero.headline: Arrest report details speeding, 0.246 blood-alcohol level in deputy's Vero Beach crash
hero.body:
St. Lucie County sheriff’s deputy Tyler Horstman, arrested Monday on a felony DUI charge tied to a March 1 crash in Vero Beach, was driving 63 mph in a 35 mph zone and had a blood-alcohol level of 0.246, according to police and his arrest report. The woman driving the other vehicle suffered a traumatic brain injury, the report says. Horstman turned himself in Monday afternoon after a felony warrant was issued, according to the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office.

The crash happened about 11:25 p.m. at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Horstman was off duty and driving an unmarked St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office pickup truck when he struck a Chevy Equinox carrying the woman and an infant, according to the arrest report. Vero Beach police said Horstman entered the intersection on a green light and the other driver entered against a red light. Both drivers were injured and taken to the hospital. The infant was alert and responsive, according to the report.

The arrest report says Horstman stated he had a few beers earlier in the evening. It describes a “faint odor of alcohol on his breath” and says he was “lethargic and dazed” and “drowsy and periodically dozing off.” The Sheriff’s Office received his blood-test results on September 9. His blood-alcohol concentration of 0.246 was more than three times Florida’s legal limit. Horstman was placed on administrative leave on September 15.

The felony warrant issued Monday lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. Horstman was booked into the Indian River County Jail at 4:59 p.m. and posted $15,000 bond at 6:24 p.m. His arraignment is scheduled for December 9. Vero Beach police are leading the criminal investigation, according to the Sheriff’s Office. The agency’s internal investigation is on hold pending the outcome of the criminal case.

It lists charges of DUI impairment involving a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury. The crash happened in March, but Horstman was not arrested until late October. "It's very typical in cases like this take months and months, and it's very frustrating for victims and their families, and also for the public, who are waiting for justice," said Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney. He is now an attorney in private practice in West Palm Beach. Aronberg says it's not unusual at all that it would take seven months for someone, in this case a Sheriff's detective, to be arrested for DUI with serious bodily injury. "Proving felony DUI with serious bodily injury requires two hard sciences. You have to have crash physics to prove causation. That's crucial to any case like this, and you also have to have toxicology to prove impairment, and neither of those things happens overnight," Aronberg said. cards.headline: Family seeks answers in St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge’s death
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s siblings say the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk after appearing normal hours earlier. They are seeking answers about his final hours.
cards.body:
The family of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died while on duty Oct. 24, says he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk early that morning and taken to a hospital. His siblings are seeking answers about his final hours and say they do not yet know what caused the 34-year-old’s death.

His sister, Alexis Hodge, said the family was told Austin had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. In addition to working as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family. “It’s a shock to literally all of us,” Alexis said. “Nobody knows what happened.”

Austin’s death came just over a year after the death of his younger brother, 26-year-old Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. They said concerns about the medical care Jairus received led Austin to seek answers and advocate for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”

Now, Alexis and Javan want to understand what happened to Austin before he was found unresponsive, including who was around him and who saw him. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. Alexis said getting answers is important to her grieving process. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Both siblings said they are determined to make Austin and Jairus proud. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a healthcare career. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County deputy charged with DUI, put on unpaid leave after Vero Beach crash
hero.body:
An off-duty St. Lucie County sheriff's detective has been charged with DUI and placed on unpaid administrative leave following a March 1 crash in Vero Beach that seriously injured a woman and hospitalized her son. Tyler Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County Jail on Monday after an investigation that took several months.

Investigators said Horstman was driving an unmarked agency pickup truck when it collided with an SUV carrying the woman and her son at Beachland Boulevard and A1A. Investigators determined that the SUV's driver ran a red light and that Horstman had a green light. They also determined that Horstman's blood alcohol level was above the legal limit. Police said his truck was traveling about 64 mph in a 35-mph zone just before the crash.

All three people involved were hospitalized. The child was later released, while the woman suffered a traumatic brain injury, according to the affidavit. The affidavit also states that Horstman said during his assessment that he had “a few beers” earlier in the evening. Police said the investigation involved search warrants, subpoenas and obtaining records.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Horstman was placed on unpaid administrative leave in accordance with agency policy. “Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process,” Del Toro said in a statement. “The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires.”

cards.headline: Indian River County sets record with 14,083 turtle nests as rough surf threatens eggs
cards.teaser: Decades of conservation helped Indian River County reach its highest nest count. Rough surf and king tides now threaten remaining nests and have delayed damage surveys.
cards.body:
Indian River County recorded a record 14,083 sea turtle nests as of Oct. 22, while rough surf and king tides threaten remaining nests and have delayed surveys to assess damage. The total surpassed the county’s previous record, set in 2023, by approximately 2,000 nests, according to Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen. Loggerheads accounted for 10,045 nests, followed by 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. Whalen said loggerheads drove much of the increase that pushed the county to its highest recorded total.

Whalen credited decades of conservation work for the milestone, including monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and efforts to encourage turtle-friendly beach practices. Along the county’s 22.4-mile coastline, orange markers identify approximately one in 10 nests. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. The markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity. Whalen said marking all 14,000 nests would leave beachgoers little room to sit. The long-term gains reflect years of work protecting both sea turtles and their nesting beaches, he said.

A nor’easter and king tides have brought powerful waves and high water as nesting season winds down. Waves strip sand from the beach, potentially exposing buried eggs, and unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween, though some nests may continue incubating beyond that date.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission advises beachgoers to leave exposed eggs in place rather than collect or rebury them. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive. Storm currents can also carry young turtles ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. People should not pick them up or return them to the ocean, but should immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance. Beachgoers can help keep nesting beaches clean, flat and dark by removing beach gear, filling holes, flattening sandcastles and keeping lights off the beach at night.

The county marks approximately one in 10 nests along its 22.4-mile coastline. If we mark 14,000 nests you wouldn’t have anywhere to sit on the beach, Whalen said. And like seriously it would be a sea of orange. Researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting turtles and their nesting beaches. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices. Rough surf threatens remaining nests A nor’easter and king tides have brought challenging conditions as nesting season winds down. Waves strip away sand, potentially exposing eggs buried beneath the beach. Unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. A lot of them have already hatched out, a lot of them have made it to the water safely, Whalen said. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween. Some nests may continue incubating beyond that date. Nesting numbers across the Treasure Coast Other counties also provided nesting figures. The totals cover different reporting dates and monitoring areas. Indian River County : As of Oct. 22, the county recorded 14,083 nests: 10,045 loggerhead, 3,970 green turtle and 68 leatherback nests. Lucie County : As of Sept. 30, the county recorded 10,239 nests: 9,111 loggerhead, 956 green turtle and 172 leatherback nests. Martin County: As of Sept. 28, its Hutchinson Island monitoring area recorded 4,874 nests: 4,532 loggerhead, 161 green turtle and 181 leatherback nests. Martin County’s figures cover approximately 7.5 miles of Hutchinson Island shoreline. That area stretches from the north side of St. Lucie Inlet to the Martin St. CBS12 News has requested Palm Beach County’s latest countywide figures from FWC and is awaiting those numbers. Boca Raton sees high nest counts, lower hatch success In Boca Raton, a strong nesting season did not translate into equally strong hatching results. David Anderson, sea turtle conservation coordinator at Gumbo Limbo Nature Center, reported the city’s third-highest nesting season. That included record counts of 1,118 loggerhead nests and 43 leatherback nests. But an average of only about 50% of the eggs in inventoried nests hatched. Anderson said a typical hatch rate would be 70% to 80% or more. He attributed some losses to prolonged hot, dry conditions during peak incubation. High sand temperatures can prevent embryos from continuing to develop. Storms and high tides also washed out approximately 185 nests, Anderson said. Predators affected another 13 nests. Artificial lighting created additional problems after hatching. Anderson said hatchlings from at least 85 nests became disoriented and headed into the dunes. Staff plan to evaluate beachfront lighting and work with nearby properties before next season. So sure, it’s sad to see so many hatchlings and eggs not fully developed, but once again, we had a great nesting season, Anderson said. So as long as the nesting numbers continue to climb, it gives us hope. What to do if you find eggs or hatchlings The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season. That strategy helps some nests survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may find exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC says to leave exposed eggs in place. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive, and people should not collect or rebury them. Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. Do not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call FWC’s 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can help by keeping beaches clean, flat and dark. Remove beach gear, fill holes, flatten sandcastles and keep lights off the beach at night.

cards.headline: Siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge’s death
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s family says the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk Saturday. His siblings are seeking answers about his final hours.
cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his final hours after the 34-year-old died in the line of duty Saturday. His family says they were told he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk early that morning and taken to a hospital.

His sister, Alexis Hodge, said the family was told Austin had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. The family is still seeking the cause of his death. “It’s a shock to literally all of us,” Alexis said. “Nobody knows what happened.”

Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. In addition to his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family. “The feeling is unbearable,” Alexis said.

Austin’s death comes just over a year after the death of his younger brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died at age 26. They said concerns about the medical care Jairus received led Austin to seek answers and advocate for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said.

Now, Alexis and Javan want to understand what happened before Austin was found unresponsive. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. Alexis said the family wants to identify who was around Austin and who saw him during his final hours. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a career in healthcare. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. Both siblings said they intend to carry on their brothers’ legacy. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said.

hero.headline: Palm City flooding makes SW Dyer Point Road impassable; rescue vehicles deployed
hero.body:
Flooding has left SW Dyer Point Road in Palm City impassable, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, which is deploying high-water rescue vehicles to help people stranded in vehicles or homes. The sheriff's office also reported flooding affecting SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue. Residents are being urged to stay away from the affected areas and to exercise extreme caution. The warning includes a reminder not to try to drive through flooded roads. Anyone who needs emergency assistance should call 911, the sheriff's office said in its notice about the flooding in Palm City.

The sheriff's office described the flooding along SW Dyer Point Road as significant and said the road cannot be passed. SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue are also among the locations affected by the flooding, according to the agency. Its warning to residents is to avoid these areas rather than attempt to travel through the floodwater. The notice identifies SW Dyer Point Road as impassable and names the other two streets as additional places experiencing flooding. For anyone considering driving in the affected areas, the sheriff's office's instruction is clear: Do not attempt to drive through a flooded roadway.

High-water rescue vehicles are being deployed to assist people who become stranded, whether they are in a vehicle or in a home, the sheriff's office said. The deployment is intended to help people in either situation as flooding affects the Palm City streets. The agency's notice pairs the rescue deployment with its request that residents avoid the flooded areas. People should not try to drive through the water, even as rescue vehicles are being sent to assist those who are stranded. The sheriff's office is urging extreme caution around the affected locations and directing anyone needing emergency assistance to call 911.

The emergency guidance applies to people who need help because of the flooding, including those stranded in their homes or vehicles. The sheriff's office directed those in need of emergency assistance to 911 and urged residents to avoid the affected areas. Its notice identifies flooding on SW Dyer Point Road, SW 34th Street and Cornell Avenue, with SW Dyer Point Road impassable. As high-water rescue vehicles are deployed to help stranded people, the agency's message to residents is to use extreme caution, stay away from those areas and never attempt to drive through floodwater.

hero.headline: Indian River County records 14,083 sea turtle nests as rough surf threatens season’s end
hero.body:
Indian River County recorded a historic 14,083 sea turtle nests as of Oct. 22, roughly 2,000 more than its previous record in 2023. Rough surf and king tides are threatening some remaining nests, while unsafe conditions have delayed surveys needed to determine the full extent of the damage.

The county’s latest dashboard lists 10,045 loggerhead nests, 3,970 green turtle nests and 68 leatherback nests. Coastal Specialist Dakota Whalen said loggerheads drove much of the increase and credited decades of conservation efforts for the milestone. Those efforts include monitoring, partnerships with conservation groups and encouraging turtle-friendly beach practices.

The orange markers beachgoers see represent only a fraction of the nesting activity along Indian River County’s 22.4-mile coastline. The county marks approximately one in 10 nests, and researchers evaluate those marked nests to help measure reproductive success. Whalen said the long-term gains reflect years of work protecting sea turtles and their nesting beaches.

A nor’easter and king tides have brought powerful waves that strip sand from beaches, potentially exposing buried eggs. Whalen estimated that 75% to 90% of the county’s nests had already hatched before the recent rough weather. Indian River County’s nesting season officially ends on Halloween, though some nests may continue incubating beyond that date.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission says sea turtles spread their nests across the season, helping some survive even when storms damage others. After rough weather, beachgoers may encounter exposed eggs or young turtles washed ashore. FWC advises leaving exposed eggs in place rather than collecting or reburying them. Eggs swept from their nests rarely survive.

Storm currents can also carry young turtles back ashore, sometimes tangled in seaweed. These washback turtles may need specialized care. FWC says people should not pick them up or return them to the ocean. Instead, immediately call its 24-hour Wildlife Alert Hotline at 888-404-3922 for instructions. Hatchlings actively crawling toward the ocean do not need assistance, according to FWC. Beachgoers can also help by removing beach gear, filling holes, flattening sandcastles and keeping lights off the beach at night.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County Detective Horstman Released on $15,000 Bond in Felony DUI Case
hero.teaser: Detective Tyler Horstman was released Monday evening after posting $15,000 bond following his surrender on a felony DUI charge tied to an off-duty crash in Vero Beach.
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office Detective Tyler Horstman, who surrendered Monday on a felony DUI charge stemming from a March 2 off-duty crash in Vero Beach, was released Monday evening after posting $15,000 bond, according to Indian River County jail records. Horstman was driving a sheriff's office vehicle when the crash occurred, Sheriff Richard Del Toro Jr. said.

Horstman turned himself in at the Indian River County Jail on Monday afternoon, Oct. 26, after a felony arrest warrant was issued. Jail records list the charge as DUI causing serious bodily injury to another. Del Toro said the warrant involved an allegation of driving under the influence with a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or higher and serious personal injury.

The Vero Beach Police Department led the criminal investigation into the March 2, 2026, crash. Del Toro said the sheriff's office learned Sept. 9 that blood testing indicated Horstman had a blood-alcohol concentration of 0.246. The sheriff said he immediately authorized an administrative investigation, and Horstman was placed on paid administrative leave Sept. 15.

After the felony warrant was issued and Horstman surrendered, he was placed on unpaid administrative leave under agency policy, Del Toro said. The sheriff's office has paused its internal investigation pending the outcome of the criminal proceedings. Vero Beach police remain the lead agency in the criminal case.

Del Toro said the allegations raise concerns for the community and the agency, which holds its personnel to high standards both on and off duty. The charge is an allegation, and Horstman's guilt or innocence has not been determined in court.

cards.headline: Siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge’s death
cards.teaser: Austin Hodge’s family says they were told he appeared normal before he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk. His siblings are seeking answers about his final hours.
cards.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his death after being told the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk early Saturday. Hodge died while on duty Oct. 24, just over a year after his younger brother, who also served with the fire district.

His sister, Alexis Hodge, said the family was told Austin had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis said the family wants to understand what happened in his final hours, including who was around him and who saw him before he was found unresponsive.

Alexis and her brother, Javan Hodge, gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. For Alexis, finding answers is part of moving forward: “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

The family is also grieving Jairus “Jay” Hodge, Austin’s 26-year-old brother. Family members said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. They said concerns about the medical care Jairus received led Austin to seek answers and advocate for his brother. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said. “He would not rest until he could spread Jay’s legacy globally.”

Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a healthcare career. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” he said. Alexis also said she intends to follow through on plans she shared with Austin. “I’m gonna do everything we talked about. And I’m gonna make him proud,” she said.

hero.headline: Martin County approves one-year data center pause; Kanner Highway proposal exempt
hero.body:
Martin County commissioners voted 4-0 Tuesday to give final approval to a one-year moratorium on new data center development. An already-filed proposal for a hyperscale data center off Kanner Highway west of Interstate 95 is exempt from the pause.

The county recently received the application for what would be its first data center, proposed in unincorporated Martin County. Because the application was submitted before the moratorium, it is exempt from the development pause.

Tuesday’s approval came at the second reading, after commissioners advanced the moratorium Oct. 13. The pause comes as county leaders consider how to handle future data center development and residents raise concerns about the facilities’ future development.

cards.headline: 15-year-old, other driver seriously hurt in U.S. Highway 1 crash after Stuart police pursuit
cards.teaser: Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce after the wrong-way collision at the Mall South Entrance intersection. Stuart police and the Florida Highway Patrol are investigating.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old driver and another motorist suffered serious injuries early Tuesday when a Stuart police pursuit ended in a wrong-way crash on U.S. Highway 1, according to the Stuart Police Department.

Officers were conducting traffic enforcement near Southwest Federal Highway and Southwest St. Lucie Crescent at about 3:45 a.m. when they spotted a vehicle traveling north at what they described as an extremely high rate of speed. An officer attempted a traffic stop, but the driver refused to stop and fled, police said.

The pursuit continued onto U.S. 1, where the driver began traveling north in the southbound lanes from Wright Boulevard, according to police. Officers continued trying to stop the vehicle because of the danger to other motorists. Police said officers also tried to alert drivers traveling on Northwest Federal Highway.

The fleeing vehicle collided with a southbound vehicle at the Mall South Entrance intersection, police said. Officers learned after the crash that the fleeing driver was 15 years old. Both drivers were taken to Lawnwood Medical Center in Fort Pierce with serious injuries.

The Stuart Police Department is investigating the incident. The Florida Highway Patrol is conducting a separate investigation into the crash.

cards.headline: King tides, strong winds flood Palm City; sheriff warns of further high water
cards.teaser: Floodwater off Dyer Point Road retreated Monday, but the sheriff’s office warned that high tide later that night could worsen conditions. Three high-water vehicles were ready for rescues.
cards.body:
Strong winds and king tides flooded parts of Palm City off Dyer Point Road on Monday, leaving some areas completely underwater. Although a resident said the water had retreated after several hours, the sheriff’s office warned that high tide later Monday night could make conditions worse and said three high-water vehicles were ready for rescues.

Terresa Baldwin, who lives off Dyer Point Road, said she also experienced flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals. Water rose over her dock and into her new patio. “The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that,” Baldwin said.

Baldwin described a sewage smell and dead copperheads in the floodwater. Even after the water went down, she remained concerned about flooding over the next few days. “The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,” Baldwin said.

Lt. Dave Rosko urged residents to think twice before driving through floodwater and said people living in coastal communities should consider future tides before traveling. “Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,” Rosko said. “If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.”

hero.headline: Austin Hodge’s siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter’s death
hero.teaser: Alexis and Javan Hodge want to understand their brother’s final hours after he was found unresponsive at his firehouse. Their family lost another firefighter brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, in July 2025.
hero.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his final hours after the 34-year-old died on duty Oct. 24. His sister, Alexis Hodge, and brother, Javan Hodge, say they want to understand what happened before he was found unresponsive in his bunk at the firehouse early Saturday. Alexis said the family had been told he appeared to be himself in the hours before he was found unresponsive, cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. Alexis and Javan gathered at Austin’s home and remembered him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family.

The siblings said they want to learn who was around Austin and who saw him before he was found unresponsive. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. For Alexis, those answers are important to moving forward with her grief. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Austin’s death came just over a year after the death of his younger brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, 26, who also served with the fire district. The family said Jairus became sick while on shift in July 2025 and later died. His medical care raised concerns for the family, and Austin sought answers and advocated for his brother, they said. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said.

Alexis and Javan said they are determined to carry on both brothers’ legacies. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue a healthcare career. He is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said. Alexis said she intends to follow through on the plans she shared with Austin: “I’m gonna do everything we talked about. And I’m gonna make him proud.”

cards.headline: Former Jensen Beach High School player Andrew Burnette gets another year at Louisiana Tech
cards.teaser: Burnette secured one more year of college football eligibility after a legal challenge against the NCAA, allowing him to return to Louisiana Tech.
cards.body:
Former Jensen Beach High School football player Andrew Burnette secured another year of college eligibility after a legal challenge against the NCAA, allowing him to return to Louisiana Tech. Burnette had exhausted his eligibility after his first season at the Division I level and spent a few months working with his father at a steel mill in Detroit before getting another chance to play.

This summer, the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, allowing student-athletes to compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. Burnette hired a lawyer and went to court against the NCAA to seek his final year of eligibility. He was granted one more year. “It was amazing; I would rather play football than do anything, and for me to have this opportunity again, it's a blessing,” said Burnette.

Burnette moved from Michigan around age 12 and played football in Martin County. He attended Jensen Beach High School originally for wrestling, then decided during high school that he wanted to pursue football. “I played football my whole life, and I can say football is a little harder in Florida than it is in Michigan,” said Burnette.

Recruiting proved difficult. “One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited,” said Burnette. He went to Highland Community College in Kansas, where he played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns. He then transferred to Independence Junior College, where he was cut from the team.

Burnette next contacted Keiser University in West Palm Beach, which had offered him a chance to play while he was in high school. After reviewing his film, a coach invited him to join the program. In two years at Keiser, Burnette rushed for more than 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns, drawing interest from Division I programs, starting with Louisiana Tech.

“Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out,” said Burnette. His successful eligibility challenge has given him another season at Louisiana Tech.

"I wasn't zoned for that school, but I went there for wrestling originally; that was my first passion," said Burnette. While he was doing well in wrestling, football kept calling to him. "Moving through high school, I knew football was what I wanted to do," said Burnette. He established himself as a force at Jensen Beach High School, but he didn't receive much interest from college football programs, similar to many Treasure Coast football recruits. "One of my main struggles was recruitment out of high school, because I felt like our area was a little under-recruited," said Burnette. Betting on himself, he decided to play at Highland Community College in Kansas. Burnette played in nine games and rushed for 340 yards and two touchdowns, but he still wasn't on any other college football program's radar. "I transferred to Independence Junior College, and I was cut from the team," said Burnette. Independence was featured on the hit Netflix show Last Chance U, but once his chance there was short-lived, he reached out to Keiser University in West Palm Beach. "I spoke with the coach there and told him, 'You guys offered me in high school,' and he said, 'I don't really remember. Send me your film.' He saw my film and said, 'Hey, bring it,'" said Burnette. And he did "bring it." In the two years he played at Keiser, he rushed for over 2,300 yards and 30 touchdowns. With stats like that, Division I programs finally came calling, starting with Louisiana Tech. "Last year I played there; it was my first year at the Division I level, and then my eligibility ran out," said Burnette. At the time, the NCAA granted student-athletes only four years of eligibility unless they were injured, so Burnette rolled up his sleeves and got to work. "I called my dad and told him, 'Hey, I need to do something. I can't just sit here,' so I went and worked with my dad in Michigan," said Burnette. He worked with his dad at a steel mill in Detroit for a few months, but this summer the NCAA announced the 5-in-5 rule, meaning student-athletes can compete for up to five seasons across a continuous five-year period. So he hired a lawyer and went to court with the NCAA to get his final year of eligibility, and they granted him one last year, and now he's making the most of it. hero.headline: Florida voters choose among Moody, Nixon and Gillespie in Senate special election
hero.body:
Early voting is underway in Florida’s special U.S. Senate election, with voters choosing among Republican incumbent Ashley Moody, Democratic challenger Angie Nixon and independent Neil Gillespie. Election Day is one week away. The winner will serve the final two years of Marco Rubio’s term. Gov. Ron DeSantis appointed Moody to the seat in January 2025 after Rubio left the Senate to become U.S. secretary of state.

Moody, a former two-term Florida attorney general from Plant City, has emphasized law enforcement and public safety, highlighting her experience as a federal prosecutor, judge and attorney general. At a recent campaign stop in Martin County with Dr. Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, she touted tax cuts enacted during President Donald Trump’s administration. Moody has described the election as a choice between “safety or chaos” and “freedom or socialism.”

Nixon, a state representative and labor organizer from Jacksonville, has centered her campaign on affordability and economic issues. She argues that working families are struggling with rising costs while politicians benefit from the current system. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America, Nixon supports a $25 minimum wage and Medicare for All and has campaigned alongside Bernie Sanders. She won a competitive Democratic primary against a more centrist opponent who significantly outraised her campaign.

Recent polling shows Moody leading by about four percentage points heading into the campaign’s final week. Florida last elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate in 2012. Gillespie is also on the ballot as an independent candidate. The special election determines who will represent Florida for the remainder of Rubio’s term, with the seat returning to the ballot in 2028.

hero.headline: Austin Hodge’s siblings seek answers after St. Lucie County firefighter’s death
hero.teaser: Alexis and Javan Hodge want to understand their brother’s final hours before he was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk Oct. 24.
hero.body:
The siblings of St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge are seeking answers about his final hours after the 34-year-old was found unresponsive in his firehouse bunk and died while on duty Oct. 24. Alexis Hodge and Javan Hodge say they want to understand what happened to their brother, whose death comes just over a year after they lost another brother who served with the fire district. Alexis said the family was told he had been cooking, talking on the phone and making jokes before going to bed. “Everybody that saw him said he was normal,” she said. That account describes what relatives were told about his behavior before he was found unresponsive, rather than an explanation for his death.

Alexis and Javan gathered at Austin’s home, remembering him as strong, fun, caring and dedicated to serving others. Along with his work as a firefighter-paramedic, Austin worked as a respiratory therapist, according to his family. “The feeling is unbearable,” Alexis said.

The siblings said their questions center on what happened before Austin was found unresponsive. “I want to know A to Z what happened,” Javan said. Alexis said the family wants to identify who was around Austin and who saw him. “After I get my answers, then I can rest and heal from my grief,” she said.

Their younger brother, Jairus “Jay” Hodge, was 26 when he died after becoming sick while on shift in July 2025, according to the family. Relatives said they had concerns about the medical care Jairus received and that Austin sought answers and advocated for him. “He would not rest until he could get to the bottom of it,” Javan said.

Now, Alexis and Javan say they intend to carry on both brothers’ legacies. Javan said Austin inspired him to pursue healthcare; he is studying to become a nurse and preparing to graduate in December. “I do know I want to make him proud. I do know I want to make both of my brothers proud,” Javan said.

hero.headline: Strong winds, king tides flood Palm City; sheriff’s office warns of more high water
hero.body:
Strong winds and king tides flooded parts of Palm City on Monday, leaving areas off Dyer Point Road underwater as the Martin County sheriff’s office warned that another high tide Monday night could worsen conditions. Three high-water vehicles were ready for rescue efforts, and residents were urged to avoid driving through flooded roads.

Dave Rosko said drivers should understand their vehicles’ limitations before entering high water. “Understand the limitations of your vehicle and do not drive through the high waters,” Rosko said. “If your vehicle gets disabled there, it may turn into a rescue event where we need to come out and ensure your safety.” He also urged residents of coastal communities to be aware of future tides before traveling.

Terresa Baldwin, who lives off Dyer Point Road, said the area was flooded for a few hours before the water retreated. She also experienced flooding in her backyard along one of the finger canals, with water covering her dock and reaching her new patio. “The wind was blowing so hard, so it was like waves crashing in your backyard, and you're like, no, nobody wants to see that,” Baldwin said.

Even as the water receded, Baldwin remained concerned about more flooding in the coming days. “The biggest concern for us is getting water from both sides. What do you do, especially when you're trying to sleep, and you don't know if the water's going to come up more or what's going to get damaged at night when you really can't see,” Baldwin said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County detective arrested on DUI charge after crash in agency vehicle
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office Detective Tyler A. Horstman was arrested Monday, Oct. 26, on a charge of DUI causing serious bodily injury to another after an off-duty crash in Vero Beach while driving an agency vehicle. Horstman turned himself in to the Indian River County jail Monday afternoon, according to the sheriff’s office.

Indian River County jail records show Horstman was released Monday evening after posting $15,000 bond. The sheriff’s office said it was notified Monday that a felony arrest warrant had been issued for driving under the influence involving impairment, a blood or breath alcohol level of 0.15 or more, and serious personal injury.

The crash occurred March 2 while Horstman was off duty and operating a St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office vehicle, according to the agency. The Vero Beach Police Department led the criminal investigation.

The sheriff’s office said it was informed that Horstman’s blood test indicated a blood alcohol concentration of 0.246. Florida’s blood alcohol limit is 0.08. After learning the test result, the sheriff immediately authorized an administrative investigation and placed Horstman on paid administrative leave, according to the agency.

“Our responsibility to uphold the law comes with an expectation that we follow it ourselves. When an employee is accused of violating that responsibility, we must address it fairly and hold them accountable through the appropriate process,” the sheriff said in a statement Monday.

“The men and women of this agency work every day to earn the trust of our community, and we will continue to hold ourselves to the standards that trust requires.”

hero.headline: Fort Pierce procession honors St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge
hero.teaser: Monday’s funeral procession traveled from the Medical Examiner’s Office to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Loved ones remembered Hodge for his positive outlook and devotion to serving his community.
hero.body:
A funeral procession for St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge, who died while on duty Oct. 24, left the Medical Examiner’s Office in Fort Pierce at 2 p.m. Monday and traveled to Stone Brothers Funeral Home. Family and friends remembered him as a source of encouragement who loved serving his community and helped others pursue careers in firefighting.

Bernard Taylor knew Hodge since their school days in Sebastian. Taylor was a senior working as a counselor at the Boys and Girls Club when he met Hodge, a freshman he mentored. Hodge always wanted to keep up with the older kids, Taylor said, and their bond lasted for years. When Taylor later decided to change careers, Hodge was one of the first people he called. Hodge answered questions and helped Taylor with conditioning as he worked toward becoming a firefighter. “Just a ball of positive energy. A smile that lights up the room. No matter what you’re going through, he had the right words to kind of get you through it,” Taylor said.

Taylor said he spoke with Hodge about a week before his death to make sure he was doing well. He said he was most heartbroken for Hodge’s mother, who has now lost both of her sons. Bonnie Hill, a family friend who helped raise Hodge’s mother, said she has been by her side. Hill said the family is relying on faith and a strong circle of support.

Hodge’s younger brother, Jarius Hodge, also a St. Lucie County Fire District firefighter and paramedic, died in July 2025 after falling ill during a shift. The district honored Jarius with line-of-duty honors. Austin spent months searching for answers after his brother’s death and pushed state lawmakers to repeal Florida’s so-called free kill law. Because Jarius was over 25 and had no spouse or children, the law barred his family from suing for medical malpractice. Austin started a petition in his brother’s honor and said his fight was about accountability, not money. Taylor said he hopes people remember Austin’s commitment to others: “He was a person who loved what he did. He was a person who loved serving his community.”
